newsitem.title: UK: Election caution hits UK-N. America airfreight.
newsitem.headline: Election caution hits UK-N. America airfreight.

text.p: The May 1 general election is causing some UK exporters of transatlantic airfreight to reduce or hold back space orders, airlines report.

Certain carriers believe customers are waiting to see if an expected election victory by the Labour party will result in a lower exchange rate, albeit for a short period, and therefore a reduction in the cost of exports, a Reuters survey shows.

"Freight forwarders tell us that the usual amount of business at this time of the year is just not there," said Phil Rawlings, Europe cargo manager of Air New Zealand, which operates London Heathrow-Los Angeles Boeing 747-400 services.

"The main reason being given to me is that because of the high value of the pound against the U.S. dollar, suppliers are holding off and waiting to see how the wind blows after the election," he added.

Peter Simmonds, UK cargo sales manager of Trans World Airlines, said his business was picking up again after experiencing a "blip" period, but he too had noticed caution on behalf of ex-UK air cargo exporters.
"The strong pound over the past two to three months has been very much to their detriment," he said.
"The value of sterling will go down if investment in Britain is affected by government industrial policies. Under old Labour practices, the pound took a pummelling and this helped exports," he said.
Simmonds felt that some customers were adopting a wait-and-see aproach in the event of this happening again in the event of a Labour victory.
But personally, both Rawlings and Simmonds -- and DHL UK managing director Nick Butcher -- felt that regardless of whether Labour or the Conservatives won the election, interest rates will go up.
"This would only strengthen the pound further as more people invest in it, and the price of exporting would continue to rise," said Simmonds.

Despite pre-election marketplace hesitancy, average per kg/100 kg ex-UK rates to North and Latin America have been increasing of late following the introduction by most airlines of traditional April 1 price hikes.

New York continues to be the most fiercely competed ex-UK route and Brian Coleman, UK cargo manager of Continental Airlines, noted it has recently been attracting some heavy spot rating -- mainly for shipments over one tonne.
Reuters enquiries show that for dense cargo consignments, per kg rates of 0.35 to 0.45 stg for a tonne and above can be obtained.
"In February, our business was ticking over, in March it was very good and in April it has picked up after a slow start due to Easter," said Coleman.
"We expect an easing down come June and the holiday season when factories close down and yet airfreight capacity increases," he added.

TWA's Simmonds felt that average UK-North America air cargo rates would be stronger than they are now if it were not for increased competition provided by carriers offering transhipment services via Continental Europe.
"While they previously used DC-9s or 727s to fly from Britain to their home airports, they now operate Airbuses and do their damndest to fill up the extra cargo space from here," he said.
"And as there is insufficient freight generated in their own markets, they allocate more and more space to UK-originating cargo on their transatlantic flights," he stated.
Market observers also point to a marked lack of full-freighters operating from Britain to North and Latin America, a situation which is being successfully exploited by certain Continental carriers.

"Because of the large number of 747 Combis we fly to North America, we are able to offer main-deck capacity (for large volume pieces) in the UK market and our payload and yield results have been very satisfactory," said a KLM Cargo spokesman from Amsterdam.

The likes of KLM should not anticipate much main-deck ex-UK competition to the Americas from national carrier British Airways in the foreseeable future, according to the latter's cargo outsourcing manager Graham Bunsell.

He said that BA was presently satisfied with the bellyold capacity it offered on flights to the U.S. and, while the carrier had operated freighters to and from Latin America in the past, "this is now on the back-burner".
Bunsell explained that BA's current ex-UK freighter priorities were the Far East, Africa and Israel.

In the U.S., Continental's Coleman said that Houston was increasing in importance as an ex-London cargo destination for his carrier, adding that competition for this market was on the rise from BA and KLM.
"We are doing well, carrying mainly oil industry-related shipments...there is a lot of exploration and maintenance underway (in Texas) requiring airfreight support," he said.

The view that Argentina is one of the fastest growing Latin American markets for airfreight from Britain was shared by Roy Douthwaite, managing director of general sales agent Air Cargo Trader, and Steve Dawkins, director of Air Logistics, LAN-Chile's UK cargo GSA.

"Along with Brazil, Argentina is very buoyant at the moment, attracting general cargo and good volumes of heavy machinery shipments for major capital projects underway there," said Douthwaite, who represents Challenge Air, Fast Air, Aeromexico, Mexicana and Aeroperu in Britain.

He added that Panama, Colombia and Chile were small but valuable ex-UK air cargo markets and Dawkins agreed that Chile was buoyant, importing increasing amounts of industrial and agricultural equipment.
Colombia will be served by a new service from the UK from May 2, when its main airline Avianca starts twice-weekly London Heathrow-Bogota Boeng 767-200 flights.
"There is plenty of trade between the UK and Colombia and I see good airfreight potential for this route," said Gil Harding, director of Avianca's new London-based cargo GSA ANA Aviation Services.

But he declined to disclose the payload capacity of the plane. This can carry much less cargo than more powerful extended-range versions of 767-200s/300s and so observers say ANA will concentrate on attracting smaller, high-yield shipments.
Also operating direct between London-Bogota is BA, but a host of carriers offer transhipment services to Colombia via Miami.
One of the biggest in this field is all-cargo Colombian carrier Tampa Airlines, in which Martinair has a 40 percent stake.

"Unlike Avianca, we go for higher weight shipments," said Richard Wright of Tampa's UK cargo GSA Globe Air Cargo, adding that he used various carriers -- including Martinair Virgin and Cargolux -- to feed Tampa's daily Miami-Colombia DC-8-71F flights.
"Business from the UK is fairly buoyant right now. It was quiet in February and began picking up last month," he noted.
Wright added that Globe also offered an ex-UK airfreight service to Panama using COPA Airlines flights from Miami. The Panama market, he described as "spasmodic".
